title: Overview and justification
body:
Almost everything you submit at university depends on the same underlying skill: turning your thinking into writing someone else can follow and be persuaded by. Essays, reports, dissertations: different formats, same core process underneath. Get better at it once, and it carries into every module that asks you to write, right through to your final degree classification.

Most people picture writing as a single act: you sit down, you write, and a finished piece appears. It almost never works like that. What actually produces good writing is a series of stages, each doing a different job, and knowing what those stages are takes a surprising amount of pressure off. When you understand that a first draft is only ever meant to be a first draft, the blank screen stops being quite so frightening.

title: Signpost
body: This is the introductory stage of Academic Writing, one of the practice areas covered across your course. This overview introduces the writing cycle as a whole, the five-stage process the rest of this course works through one stage at a time.

title: The writing cycle
instruction: Select each stage to find out what it does.
mobileInstruction: Select the plus icon followed by the next arrow to explore each stage.

_graphic.alt: The writing cycle: a circular diagram showing five stages in order: 1. Understand the task, 2. Plan, 3. Draft, 4. Edit, 5. Proofread. Arrows connect each stage to the next, with the final stage looping back to earlier stages, showing that the cycle is iterative rather than strictly linear.
_graphic.attribution: PLACEHOLDER — replace with final writing-cycle diagram artwork

_items.title: 1. Understand the task
_items.body: The first stage works out what you're being asked to do. Before you write a word, you need to know what the question is really asking: what's the steer, what are the keywords, and what kind of response is expected. Getting this right shapes everything that follows.

_items.title: 2. Plan
_items.body: Planning decides what you'll say and in what order. A clear plan means you're not trying to invent your argument and your sentences at the same time. Even a rough outline makes the drafting far easier.

_items.title: 3. Draft
_items.body: The first draft gets it down, roughly. Its job is to turn your plan into prose, not to be perfect. A draft you can improve is worth far more than a blank page you're still staring at.

_items.title: 4. Edit
_items.body: Editing improves what's there. This is where you reshape paragraphs, sharpen your argument, and check that your writing actually answers the question. Editing often sends you back to your plan, and that's fine.

_items.title: 5. Proofread
_items.body: Proofreading catches the final errors: spelling, punctuation, formatting, and references. It's a separate stage because it needs fresh eyes, ideally after a break from writing.

title: Signpost (continued)
body: It's the foundation for everything else in this course; each stage gets a closer look of its own in the topics ahead: understanding the task, planning, drafting, editing, proofreading, and the errors that trip students up most often. Each builds on the one before it, so the order matters more than any single topic on its own.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Explain how the stages of the writing cycle relate to one another, from understanding the task through to proofreading.
  • Identify a stuck point at any stage of the cycle and describe a practical response to it, rather than stopping.
  • Recognise common technical errors in student writing, and distinguish editing from proofreading.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this topic, you will be able to:

  • Distinguish between a question's steer (the instruction) and its keywords (the subject matter).
  • Read an assessment question in a way that reveals what it's actually asking you to do.
  • Identify hidden words in a question that shape the task even when they're easy to overlook.

title: Orientation
body:
Before you write a single sentence of an assignment, there's a step that shapes everything that follows: working out what the task is actually asking of you. It's tempting to skip it. When a deadline is looming and the blank screen is staring back at you, the instinct is to start writing and hope the meaning becomes clear along the way. But a piece of writing that misreads the question rarely recovers, however well written it is. Your tutor marks the task you were set, not the one you drifted into answering instead; the few minutes you spend understanding the task at the start are what keep the rest of your effort pointing in the right direction.

Understanding the task is the first stage of the writing cycle, the sequence that carries a piece of work from a question to a finished draft. It's worth slowing down here, because a small misreading at this stage turns into a large problem later on.

title: Concept example
body: Take a question like this one: 'Assess the effectiveness of neighbourhood policing in reducing burglary.' Two things in it are doing most of the work. The opening word, 'Assess', is telling you how to answer: it's asking you to weigh something up and reach a view, not simply describe it. The words that follow, 'effectiveness', 'neighbourhood policing', 'burglary', are telling you what that judgement is about, and how narrow its boundaries are.

title: Concept definition
body: These two elements have names. The opening word or phrase is the steer: the part of the question that points to the approach you need to take, and often to the particular skill being tested. The content words are the keywords: the terms that fix the subject and scope of your response. Almost every assessment question you meet can be read this way, by separating what it's asking you to do from what it's asking you to do it about. Once you can see both, the question stops being a wall of words and becomes a set of instructions.

title: Worked example: {{character.name}} reads the question
body: Let's see how this works on a real question. Rhian, a second-year criminology student, has been set the following task. Select each heading to follow how she reads it, one part at a time.
instruction: Select the headings to follow {{character.name}}'s reasoning.

_items.title: She reads the question, not the topic
_items.body: Rhian reads her essay question: 'To what extent does poverty explain rising youth knife crime in England and Wales?' Her first instinct is to open a blank document and start writing everything she knows about knife crime. Instead, she stops and looks at the question itself.

_items.title: The steer: 'To what extent'
_items.body: She starts with the opening phrase. 'To what extent', she decides, is asking her to reach a judgement, to weigh how far poverty explains the problem rather than just describing the problem itself.

_items.title: The obvious keywords
_items.body: Then she looks at the rest. 'Poverty', 'youth knife crime' and 'England and Wales' are the obvious keywords; they tell her what the essay is about and where its boundaries sit.

_items.title: The hidden word: 'explain'
_items.body: But two smaller words catch her eye. The question doesn't ask what poverty is linked to; it asks what poverty 'explains', which pushes her towards causes, and towards weighing poverty against other possible explanations.

_items.title: The hidden word: 'rising'
_items.body: And it doesn't ask about knife crime in general; it asks about 'rising' knife crime, which means she'll need to account for a change over time, not just a snapshot.

title: Analysis
body: What Rhian does here is exactly what the steer and keywords are for. By starting with 'To what extent', she settles the approach before she settles the content; she now knows the essay has to reach a judgement about how far poverty explains the rise, which is a very different task from describing knife crime or simply listing its causes. That one decision shapes everything she plans next. Her handling of the keywords is just as telling. She sees that the obvious terms, 'poverty', 'youth knife crime', 'England and Wales', mark out the territory, but that some of the real steer sits in the smaller words. 'Explain' quietly commits her to causes, and to weighing poverty against other explanations; 'rising' quietly commits her to a trend over time, not a single moment. Reading a question at this level takes a few minutes. Misreading it can cost you a grade band, because you can write a genuinely strong essay that answers a question you were never asked.

title: Formative check: identifying the steer
body: In Rhian's essay question, 'To what extent does poverty explain rising youth knife crime in England and Wales?', which word or phrase is the steer?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which word or phrase is the steer in this essay question?

_items.text: To what extent
poverty
explain
rising

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'To what extent' is the steer because it appears at the opening and tells you how to answer: reach a judgement about how far poverty explains the rise, rather than simply describing the problem.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The steer is the opening word or phrase that tells you how to approach the question. Look again at where the question begins.
_incorrect.final: The steer is 'To what extent'. It sits at the very start of the question and tells Rhian she needs to reach a judgement, not just describe. The other options, 'poverty', 'explain' and 'rising', are all important, but they're keywords or hidden steers within the content, not the opening steer that sets the whole approach.

title: Practical guidance
body:
You can apply the same approach to any assessment task you're given. It comes down to three habits, worth building now while the stakes are still relatively low.

  1. Find the steer and the keywords. Mark the opening word or phrase, then the terms that define the subject; separating the two is what turns a question into instructions.
  2. Work out what the steer is asking of you. 'Assess', 'To what extent', 'Discuss' and 'Compare' each call for a different kind of answer, so decide what kind of thinking the steer is testing before you start to plan.
  3. Read the marking criteria alongside the question. The criteria, usually in the assessment brief or on Moodle, tell you what your tutor is actually rewarding; reading them now means you plan towards them rather than guessing at them later.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about an assignment you've got coming up, or one you've recently handed in. What's its steer, and did you work out what it was really asking you to do before you started writing? There's no right or wrong answer here; the point is just to notice whether you read the task, or only the topic.
instruction: If you'd like, jot down your thoughts below. This is for your own reflection and won't be marked. Select Submit to save your response; it'll be here when you return.

title: Summary
body: Every assessment question contains two things: a steer that tells you what to do, and keywords that tell you what to do it about. Finding both before you start writing is a small investment that shapes everything that follows. The next topic picks up from here: once you know what the question is asking, the next step is building a plan that will guide your answer.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this topic, you will be able to:

  • Describe the purpose of a plan as the link between your research and your written work.
  • Identify the core elements a plan should set out: introduction, main part, and conclusion.
  • Distinguish a live, evolving plan from a fixed one you write once and leave unchanged.

title: Orientation
body: You've already seen, in the last topic, how to work out what an essay question is actually asking. Once you know that, the next question is what you're going to say in response, and in what order. That's what planning does. It sits between the research you've done and the writing you're about to start, and it's easy to skip, especially when a deadline feels close and typing feels like progress. This topic looks at why that shortcut usually costs you more time than it saves, and shows you how to build a plan that actually earns its place in the writing cycle.

title: Concept introduction
body:
A plan is the bridge between your research and your writing. Without one, you're trying to do two difficult things at once: work out what you think, and find the words for it. Separating those tasks is what makes the writing stage easier, and a plan is what makes that separation possible.

A good plan isn't a document you write once and leave alone. Think of it more as a sandpit: somewhere to move ideas around, delete what no longer earns its place, and test out how a sentence or a paragraph might eventually read, before you commit to writing it properly. That's a different way of thinking about planning than most students arrive at university with, where a "plan" often means a fixed list made in five minutes before the real work starts.

title: Worked example: weaker approach
body:
Natalie has an assignment due in ten days. The night before she'd planned to start writing, she opens a blank document and, in about five minutes, jots down a list: introduction, three points, conclusion. Satisfied it's sorted, she closes the document and doesn't look at it again until she sits down to write, two days later.
When she opens her draft, the plan doesn't tell her much. The three points are broad, and she can't quite remember what she meant to say under each one. She's read more since making the list, and some of what she now knows doesn't fit the original three points at all. Rather than changing the plan, she abandons it and starts writing from memory instead.

title: Analysis: weaker approach
body: Natalie's plan wasn't a bad idea; it stopped working the moment she stopped updating it. Written once and left alone, it couldn't hold what she'd learned since making it, so by the time she needed it, it had nothing useful left to offer. The problem isn't that she planned. It's that she treated the plan as finished before her thinking was.

title: Worked example: stronger approach
body:
Jess is writing a report assessing whether social media is worth the investment for a typical small or medium-sized enterprise (SME). Before drafting a single paragraph, she opens a blank document and starts building her plan.
She sets out three sections: introduction, main part, conclusion. Under the introduction, she drafts a rough line of reasoning: her provisional answer to the question, even though she knows it might shift as she reads more. Under the main part, she doesn't write prose yet; she lists the questions her report needs to answer: how widely is social media actually used by SMEs, what does the research say about its benefits and drawbacks, and where has it worked well or badly in practice. Under the conclusion, she sketches where she thinks the evidence is pointing (not a final answer, just a working one).
Two days later, having read three more sources, Jess comes back to the plan and changes her introduction's line of reasoning. The evidence is more mixed than she first thought. She doesn't start again; she edits what's there.

title: Analysis: stronger approach
body: Notice the difference. Jess's plan does the same basic job as Natalie's (three sections, a rough shape), but she treats it as something she can come back to and change. When new reading complicates her thinking, she edits the plan rather than abandoning it, so by the time she starts writing, it still reflects what she actually knows. That's the difference a live plan makes: not more effort to produce, but a different relationship with the document once it exists.

title: Practical guidance
body:
When you build your own plan:

  1. Set out the three core elements first: introduction, main part, conclusion, even before you know exactly what will go in each one.
  2. Under the introduction, draft a provisional line of reasoning: your current best answer to the question. Expect it to change.
  3. Under the main part, list the questions or points your work needs to cover, rather than writing full sentences at this stage.
  4. Treat the plan as live. Come back to it as you read more, and change it without treating that as starting over.
  5. Use the plan itself as low-stakes practice for your sentence structure and expression, before you're writing to be marked.

title: Check your understanding
body:
A student preparing an essay on climate policy has two documents open. One reads: "Intro, carbon tax pros/cons, conclusion, maybe mention Paris Agreement somewhere?" The other reads: "Introduction: set out the core tension between economic cost and environmental benefit. Main part: (1) What is a carbon tax and how does it work? (2) What do economists say about its effectiveness? (3) What are the main objections? Conclusion: weigh the evidence and offer a qualified judgement."

Which document is the properly-shaped plan?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of the two documents described is the properly-shaped plan?

_items.text: The first document, because it's shorter and leaves room to add detail later.
The second document, because it sets out introduction, main part, and conclusion with clear questions to answer.
Both are equally good plans, just at different stages of development.
Neither is a proper plan, because a plan should be written after the first draft.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second document is a properly-shaped plan because it sets out the three core elements (introduction, main part, conclusion) and, under each one, identifies what that section needs to do. The first document is closer to a rough list of topics than a plan you could actually write from.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at what each document actually tells you about how to write the essay. One of them sets out the three core elements and what each section needs to cover; the other is more of a topic list. Have another look.
_incorrect.final: The second document is the properly-shaped plan. It sets out introduction, main part, and conclusion, and under each one it identifies the questions or jobs that section needs to do. The first document is a rough list of topics, but it doesn't give you a structure you could actually write from. A good plan bridges your research and your writing by telling you what goes where.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about how you've planned written work in the past, if you have at all. Did it look more like {{character.name}}'s live, evolving plan, or more like a fixed list made quickly before the writing itself? There's no right or wrong answer here; it's worth noticing before you try the live-plan approach for yourself.
instruction: If you'd like, jot down your thoughts below. This is for your own reflection and won't be marked. Select Submit to save your response; it'll be here when you return.

title: Summary
body: Planning is what turns research into writing you can actually start. Set out the shape early, keep it live as your thinking develops, and use it as a space to practise your expression before it counts. The next topic picks up where the plan leaves off: turning it into an actual first draft.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this topic, you will be able to:

  • Explain what a first draft is for within the writing cycle.
  • Identify a writing trap when it happens, and describe the practical response to one.
  • Distinguish the purpose of drafting (getting the work down) from the purpose of editing (improving what's there).

title: Orientation
body: You've got a plan. Now comes the part that can feel like the real test: turning it into actual sentences. It's tempting to treat the first draft as though it needs to be right first time, but that's not what this stage is for. This topic looks at what a first draft is actually meant to achieve, and what to do when you get stuck partway through, which happens to almost everyone.

title: Concept introduction
body:
A first draft has one job: to exist. Not to be good, not to be close to finished, just to be there, so the next stages of the cycle have something to work with. That's a genuinely different aim from the finished piece you'll eventually submit, and holding onto that distinction is what stops drafting from feeling like a test you can fail.

Your plan is what turns this from staring at a blank page into something more manageable: you already know, roughly, what goes where. The job now is just to fill it in.

title: Worked example: weaker approach
body: Natalie sits down to draft her report. She doesn't have a plan to work from (she abandoned it days ago), so she starts at the introduction and tries to get it right straight away. Ten minutes pass. She rewrites the first sentence four times, deletes the paragraph, and starts again. Nothing sounds right. Twenty minutes later, she's produced two sentences and closed the document, frustrated.

title: Analysis: weaker approach
body: Natalie isn't drafting; she's editing a draft that doesn't exist yet. Trying to make the introduction perfect before anything else is written is a writing trap: a point where forward progress stalls because the bar for "good enough to continue" has been set too high, too early. Without a plan to fall back on, she has nowhere else to go when the introduction won't come, so she stays stuck on it.

title: Worked example: stronger approach
body: Jess sits down to draft her report, plan open beside her. She starts on the introduction and, like Natalie, finds the line of reasoning isn't quite coming together in sentence form. After a few minutes of not getting anywhere, she stops trying to force it, scrolls to the main part of her plan, and starts drafting the section on how widely SMEs actually use social media instead, a part she has clearer evidence for. Forty minutes later she has a rough draft of two sections. She comes back to the introduction last, once the rest of the report has clarified what she's actually arguing.

title: Analysis: stronger approach
body: Jess hits the same snag Natalie does (the introduction not coming easily), but her plan gives her somewhere else to go. Moving to a different section isn't giving up on the introduction; it's recognising that a stuck sentence doesn't have to stop the whole session. By the time she returns to it, she has more of the report written, which makes the introduction easier to draft, not harder.

title: Practical guidance
body:
When you're drafting:

  1. Aim to get a complete draft down, however rough. It isn't the finished piece; there's an editing stage to come.
  2. Use your plan to keep the draft structured as you go, section by section.
  3. If a section won't come, don't sit with it. Move to a different part of your plan and come back to the stuck section later.

title: Check your understanding
body: A student is drafting an essay. They've been stuck on the same paragraph for twenty minutes: rewriting it, deleting it, starting again. Nothing sounds right. What's the best next step?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the best next step when stuck on the same paragraph for twenty minutes?

_items.text: Keep trying to fix the same paragraph until it's right.
Delete the whole draft and start again from scratch.
Move to a different section of the plan and return to this paragraph later.
Stop writing for the day and come back tomorrow.

_feedback.correct: That's right. When a section won't come, the practical response is to move to a different part of your plan rather than staying stuck. A rough draft of another section is more useful than twenty more minutes staring at the same paragraph, and you can always return to it later.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the lesson said about writing traps and how to respond to them. What did {{character.name}} do when the introduction wouldn't come? Have another look.
_incorrect.final: The best next step is to move to a different section of the plan and return later. Staying stuck on one paragraph is a writing trap; deleting the whole draft throws away work you've already done; and stopping for the day means no progress at all. Moving to a section you can draft keeps the session productive, and you can come back to the stuck paragraph once you've written more.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a time you got stuck partway through a piece of writing. What did you do: keep pushing at the same spot, stop altogether, or move to something else? There's no right or wrong answer; it's worth noticing which one you default to.
instruction: If you'd like, jot down your thoughts below. This is for your own reflection and won't be marked. Select Submit to save your response; it'll be here when you return.

title: Summary
body: A first draft only has to exist, not to be good. Use your plan to keep it structured, and when a section won't come, move on rather than staying stuck. Once you've got a complete rough draft, the next stage is making it stronger, which is what editing is for.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this topic, you will be able to:

  • Distinguish editing from proofreading.
  • Identify specific ways a paragraph can be edited to argue more clearly.
  • Recognise how words like "however" and "therefore" signal a critical edge, showing the relationship between ideas rather than just listing them.

title: Orientation
body: You've got a complete draft. It won't be your best work yet, and it isn't meant to be; that's what this stage is for. Editing is where you go back through what you've written and make it genuinely stronger: not fixing typos, but improving how the argument itself holds together.

title: Concept introduction
body:
Editing and proofreading get confused because they both happen after the draft, but they're doing different jobs. Proofreading catches typos and formatting slips, and it's coming up next. Editing is bigger than that: adding text, cutting it, restructuring a paragraph, changing how an idea is expressed. It's where a draft that says roughly the right things becomes a piece of writing that says them well.

One thing to look for specifically: whether you're just reporting what your sources say, or using them to build your own point. That second move (using evidence to support an argument rather than listing it) is what gives writing a critical edge, and editing is where you can put it in.

title: Before editing
instruction: Select each marked phrase to see the commentary.

_passage.text: [UNMERGED: passage content comes from the context pack]

title: After editing
instruction: Select each marked phrase to see the commentary.

_passage.text: [UNMERGED: passage content comes from the context pack]

title: Analysis
body: Both paragraphs contain the same facts. The difference is what Jess did with them. The first version reports one source after another (this happened, then this, then this) without saying how they relate. The edited version shows the reader how those sources fit together into one argument, not just a pile of separate facts. That's the critical edge: not different content, but a different relationship between Jess and the evidence she's using.

title: Practical guidance
body:
When you're editing:

  1. Read your full draft through once it's complete, before making any changes.
  2. Look for paragraphs that report sources one after another without connecting them; that's where a critical edge is usually missing.
  3. Use words like "however," "yet," and "therefore" to show the relationship between your points, not just to list them.
  4. Make substantive changes at this stage: restructure, cut, add. Leave typos and formatting for proofreading, next.

title: Check your understanding
body:
Read the two versions of a paragraph below. Both report the same two facts.

Version A: "Research shows that student engagement increases when lectures are interactive. Many lecturers have adopted active learning techniques in recent years."

Version B: "Research shows that student engagement increases when lectures are interactive. However, many lecturers still rely primarily on traditional lecture formats."

Which version shows a critical edge, and which word does the work?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which version shows a critical edge, and which word does the work?

_items.text: Version A: the relationship is clear without a connecting word
Version A: listing facts without commentary shows objectivity
Version B: "However" signals the relationship
Version B: "still" signals the relationship

_feedback.correct: That's right. Version B shows a critical edge because "However" signals a contrast between what the research says and what lecturers actually do. The word shows the reader how the two facts relate, rather than leaving them to infer it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. One version explicitly shows how its two facts relate to each other; the other just lists them. Which word does that connecting work? Have another look.
_incorrect.final: Version B shows the critical edge, and "However" does the work. It signals a contrast: research points one way, but practice doesn't follow. "Still" adds emphasis, but "However" is the word that connects the two facts. Version A lists the same kind of information without showing how the facts relate.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look back at something you've written recently. Does it mostly report what your sources say, or does it use them to build your own point? There's no right or wrong answer; it's just worth noticing before your next edit.
instruction: If you'd like, jot down your thoughts below. This is for your own reflection and won't be marked. Select Submit to save your response; it'll be here when you return.

title: Summary
body: Editing is where a draft becomes an argument: restructuring, connecting ideas, and giving your evidence a critical edge rather than just reporting it. Once the substance is right, the final stage is proofreading: catching the surface-level errors that are easy to fix once everything else is in place.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this topic, you will be able to:

  • Distinguish proofreading from editing.
  • Identify the kinds of errors proofreading is meant to catch.
  • Describe a practical proofreading routine you can apply to your own work.

title: Orientation
body: You've made the substantive changes. What's left is smaller in scale but still matters: catching the typos, formatting slips, and small errors that survive editing because they're easy to miss when you already know what you meant to write. This topic looks at how to actually catch them.

title: Concept introduction
body: Proofreading is the last stage of the cycle, and it's tempting to treat it as optional once a deadline is close: a quick read-through, if there's time. But superficial errors are exactly the kind of thing a marker notices even when the underlying argument is strong, and they're also the easiest kind of error to fix, provided you leave room for them. The core idea is simple: proofread with fresh eyes, not straight after editing, and check for one kind of thing at a time rather than everything at once.

title: Worked example: weaker approach
body: Natalie finishes editing her report late the night before it's due. She reads it through once, quickly, and submits it straight away; there's no time left for anything else. The version she submits has a comma splice in the second paragraph, a reference cited one way in the text and a slightly different way in the reference list, and a typo in a section heading.

title: Analysis: weaker approach
body: None of Natalie's errors are serious on their own, but together they give the impression of work that wasn't quite finished. The problem isn't that she made mistakes (everyone does); it's that editing straight into submission left no room to catch them. Proofreading needs its own separate pass, not to be squeezed into the tail end of editing.

title: Worked example: stronger approach
body: Jess finishes editing her report the evening before it's due, and deliberately leaves the proofread until the next morning. She reads it through once for sense and typos, then a second time specifically checking that every in-text citation matches the reference list exactly. On the second pass, she notices she's used a comma where the sentence really needs a full stop (the same pattern, twice, in different paragraphs) and fixes both.

title: Analysis: stronger approach
body: Jess's advantage isn't that she's a better writer than Natalie; it's that she treats proofreading as its own task, done separately and with a gap before it. Reading once for meaning and once for reference formatting catches things a single quick read-through won't, and coming back the next morning means she's reading what's actually on the page, not what she remembers writing.

title: Practical guidance
body:
1. Leave a genuine gap between editing and proofreading: even a few hours helps you read what's there, not what you meant to write.
  2. Read once for meaning and typos, then again specifically for reference formatting: one pass per concern, not everything at once.
  3. Reading slowly, sentence by sentence, catches more than skimming.
  4. Aim for fewer errors, not zero. No piece of writing is perfect.

title: Check your understanding
body:
Below are two short excerpts from student essays. One has been proofread; the other has not.

Excerpt A:
"Recent studies suggest that sleep deprivation affects cognitive performence significantly (Walker, 2017). title: Summary
body: Proofreading is a separate task from editing: a fresh-eyes check for typos, formatting, and reference consistency, done with a gap after editing rather than folded into it. title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this topic, you will be able to:

  • Identify the five most common technical errors in student writing.
  • Recognise each error type in a piece of writing, including your own.
  • Distinguish a comma splice from a correctly formed sentence boundary.

title: Orientation
body: You now know how to catch errors when you proofread. This topic looks at exactly which errors to look for: the five that come up most often in student writing, based on years of marking. Knowing the list in advance makes proofreading faster, because you're checking for something specific rather than reading and hoping something jumps out.

title: Concept introduction
body: These five errors aren't equally common. The list runs from least to most frequent, and the most common one by some distance is the comma splice: two complete sentences joined with a comma instead of a full stop. That matters for where you focus your attention. If proofreading time is short, checking for a comma splice first catches the single most likely error in any given piece of writing.

title: Analysis
body: This short paragraph has three of the five errors in it. "Social media marketing is a useful tool for SMEs, however it's not always easy" is a comma splice; "however" is joining two complete sentences, so it needs a full stop or semicolon before it, not a comma. "Many businesses don't have the resource's to run a full campaign, this means smaller platforms" has both an apostrophe error ("resource's" should be "resources," no apostrophe needed) and another comma splice. "SME's" and "its easier" show the same apostrophe confusion twice more: "SMEs" needs no apostrophe (plural, not possessive), while "it's" (it is) does. None of these are complicated once you know what you're looking for; they're just easy to miss in your own writing, because you know what you meant.

title: Practical guidance
body:
The full list, from least to most common:

  1. Apostrophe misuse. Missing where needed ("SMEs report" not "SME's"), or added where not ("its easier" should be "it's," meaning "it is"). Check every apostrophe: is it showing possession, or a missing letter, or has it been added out of habit?
  2. Semicolon/colon confusion. A semicolon joins two related complete sentences; a colon introduces a list or explanation. If you can replace it with "and" or a full stop, it's doing a semicolon's job. If it's introducing something, it's doing a colon's job.
  3. Missing or wrong articles ("a," "an," "the"). More common if English isn't your first language, but everyone misses these occasionally. Read the sentence aloud; a missing article usually sounds wrong before you can say why.
  4. Overlong or overcomplicated sentences. If a sentence needs reading twice to follow, it's probably trying to do too much. Split it in two.
  5. Comma splices. By far the most common. Two complete sentences, joined with a comma instead of a full stop or semicolon. Test: could each half stand alone as its own sentence? If yes, a comma alone isn't enough to join them.

title: Course summary
body:
That's the introductory stage of Academic Writing complete: the writing cycle from planning through to catching the errors that trip people up most often. The assessment you've just done checked whether the stages hang together as a whole, not just whether you'd followed each topic on its own.

Whatever your result, the stages themselves don't stop being useful once the assessment's done. Planning before you write, treating a first draft as a working document rather than a finished one, editing for a critical edge before you proofread for typos: these are habits worth keeping, not a one-off checklist for this course alone.

title: In real academic practice
body: Everything this course has covered is the working routine behind every assessed piece you will produce at university: reading the task closely, planning before you write, drafting without chasing perfection, editing for substance, and proofreading for surface errors. Tutors see the difference immediately; work that has been through the cycle reads as considered, while work that went straight from first draft to submission rarely does. The same routine carries beyond university into any role where your writing represents your thinking to people who were not in the room.

title: Where this goes next
body: The intermediate stage builds on this foundation with techniques for enhancing your writing: sharpening how you express ideas, strengthening how your work is structured, and bringing sources into your argument rather than alongside them. If the Common errors lesson's pointer to those techniques caught your interest, that is where it leads.
